Daniel’s Windows
DAN-yuhlz WIN-dohz
proper noun
From Daniel 6:10, where Daniel prayed with his windows open toward Jerusalem despite the royal decree.

Biblical Definition

Daniel’s windows are the open casements of Daniel 6:10, through which the aged prophet prayed toward Jerusalem three times a day, and they have become a figure of holy courage and steadfast devotion in the face of a wicked decree. The presidents and princes, envious of Daniel, had persuaded King Darius to sign an unalterable decree that for thirty days no man should ask a petition of any god or man save the king, on pain of the lions’ den. When Daniel knew the writing was signed, he did not hide, nor did he flaunt; he went into his house, and his windows being open in his chamber toward Jerusalem—as was his custom—he kneeled upon his knees three times a day and prayed and gave thanks before his God, as he did aforetime. He changed nothing. He prayed toward Jerusalem as Solomon had bidden the exiles pray toward the city and house God had chosen; he kept the hours of evening, morning, and noon that the psalmist kept; and he obeyed God rather than men. The dictionary reads Daniel’s windows as the emblem of faithful prayer that will not be silenced by the powers of the age: not reckless display, but settled, habitual, unhidden devotion that continues as before when the cost is the lions’ den.

Webster 1828 Definition

From Daniel 6:10; the prophet’s windows open toward Jerusalem, through which he prayed three times a day despite the royal decree—the emblem of steadfast, unhidden devotion.

Act 5:29 — "Then Peter and the other apostles answered and said, We ought to obey God rather than men."

1Ki 8:48 — "And so return unto thee with all their heart, and with all their soul, in the land of their enemies, which led them away captive, and pray unto thee toward their land, which thou gavest unto their fathers, the city which thou hast chosen, and the house which I have built for thy name:"

Modern Corruption

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition, though the age that would push faith out of public life is rebuked by a prophet who would not close his windows.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle the open windows press upon every age is the steadfastness of public, habitual devotion when the powers forbid it. Daniel did not invent a new boldness for the crisis nor retreat into a private faith that no one could see; he simply continued as he did aforetime, kneeling toward Jerusalem with his windows open. The secular age that would privatize religion, pushing prayer and confession out of public life on pain of penalty, meets in Daniel a quiet, unanswerable defiance: he obeyed God rather than men, and he did it openly, at the appointed hours, as always.

The principle to recover is settled, costly, unhidden prayer. Daniel’s courage was the fruit of a long habit—evening, morning, and noon, as the psalmist sang—not a sudden heroism. The believer who would stand in the day of decree must pray as Daniel prayed before it, with windows open, hours kept, knees bent, giving thanks. When obedience to God collides with the decrees of men, the faithful keep their windows open and trust God with the lions.
